Recoveries between 97.9% and 102.5% were found from jelly, fruit pastel, Smarties, ice cream, and candy. Hydrophobic DESs based on hexafluoroisopropanol and 1- carnitine/betaine were used as extraction solvents for the dispersive liquid-liquid microextraction of pyrethroids.70 More specifically, the hydrophobic DESs were hexafluoroisopropanol with betaine and L-carnitine in 2:1, 2.5:1, and 3:1 molar ratios. The pyrethroids tested were transfluthrin, fenpropathrin, fenvalerate, ethofenpox, and bifenthrin, removed from tea beverages and fruit juices. The results showed that recoveries varied between 85.1% and 109.4%. The latest work on the use of hydrophobic DESs in combination with ultrasound-assisted dispersive liquid–liquid microextraction investigated pyrethroid insecticides in environmental water. 39 The pyrethroid samples investigated were deltamethrin, fenvalerate, permethrin, etofenprox, and bifenthrin, while river water and lake water were used as the aqueous phase. For the DES phases, octanoic, decanoic, and dodecanoic acid were mixed with (tetradecyl)phosphonium tetrafluoroborate. Varying parameters, including pH value, sample volume, and salt addition were tested. The recovery ranges varied between 80.93% and 109.88%. ## Microextractions Based on Solidification of Floating Drops. Since hydrophobic DESs have been described as interesting replacements for traditional solvents, research has been performed in microextractions that are based on the solidification of floating drops for the removal of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons from water.65 More specifically, the carboxylic acids acetic, decanoic, acrylic, octanoic, propionic, oleic, and butyric acid were prepared in combination with tetrabutylammonium bromide in a 2:1 molar ratio of acid to the quaternary ammonium salt. The polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons were naphthalene, fluorene, phenanthrene, anthracene, fluranthene, and pyrene. Different parameters influencing the microextraction parameters were varied, for example, extraction temperature and sample volume. It was concluded that decanoic acid:tetrabutylammonium bromide (2:1) performed the most desirable. The microextraction research with hydrophobic DESs continued when salol:DL-menthol in a 1:1 molar ratio was researched in a microextraction method where a settled organic drop was solidified.60 Four components were mixed with menthol in a 1:1 ratio, i.e., octanoic acid, decanoic acid, oleic acid, and salol. Salol:DL-menthol (1:1) was stated as a ultrahydrophobic DES with as properties a low viscosity and melting and freezing points and was chosen for the extraction experiments. Extractions of 2-nitrotoluene, 3-nitrotoluene, nitrobenzene, 1,3-dinitrobenzene, 1,3,5-trinitrobenzene, 2,6- dinitrotoluene, 2,4-dinitrotoluene, and 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene were investigated. After optimization of different factors, such as extraction temperature and DES composition and volume, recoveries between 89% and 105% were achieved. The DES prepared in a 1:1 molar ratio between decanoic acid and choline chloride is used to determine the amount of lead in food and water samples by floating organic droplet micro- extraction. 44 The recovery rate was 95%, and the relative standard deviation was 4.2%. **Ultrasound-Assisted Emulsification Liquid Phase Microextraction.** Another application in which hydrophobic DESs and microextraction were combined was the digestion and ultrasound-assisted emulsification liquid phase microextraction of copper in liver samples.72 Seven of the eight DESs could be considered as hydrophilic, while the DES consisting of decanoic acid and tetrabutylammonium chloride in a 2:1 ratio can be considered as a hydrophobic one. Eventually, the hydrophobic DES was the most successful with a recovery percentage up to 100%. Another application of the combination of hydrophobic DESs with ultrasound-assisted extraction was the removal of lycopene from tomato processing wastes. 73 Menthol was mixed in an 8:1 molar ratio with lactic acid to form a hydrophobic DES. Shaker-Assisted Liquid–liquid Microextraction. Shaker-assisted liquid–liquid microextraction using hydrophobic DESs was used to remove methylene blue from alkaline solutions (0.5 M NaOH).³⁴ It was back-extracted into a solution consisting of hydrochloric acid (2 M). The DES used throughout the investigation was decanoic acid with methyl-trioctylammonium bromide in a 2:1 molar ratio. Recovery rates between 95.91% and 102.96% were found from wastewater and river water. ## Formation of a Two Phase System of Hydrophilic and Hydrophobic DESS. It was tested if a two phase system of a hydrophilic and hydrophobic DESs could be used for the extraction of bioactive compounds from *Ginkgo biloba* leaves. 56 As hydrophobic DESs, the ternary system composed of methyltrioyctylammonium chloride, capryl alcohol, and octylic acid in a 1:2:3 molar ratio was used. Three hydrophilic DESs were tested in the formation of hydrophilic-hydrophobic two phase systems, namely, levulinic acid:choline chloride (2:1) with a water content of 40%, ethylene glycol:betaine (3:1) with a water content of 40%, and malonic acid:choline chloride (2:1) with 55% of water. By mixing a hydrophobic DES with a hydrophilic DES in a 1:1 volume ratio, the two phase systems were prepared. The hydrophilic phases were single DESs or combinations of lactic acid:choline chloride (2:1) and ethylene glycol:betaine (3:1), levulinic acid:choline chloride (2:1) and malonic acid:choline chloride (2:1), or ethylene glycol:betaine (3:1) and malonic acid:choline chloride (2:1). The bioactive compounds evaluated were Ginkgo flavonoids, terpene trilactones, procyanidine, and polyprenyl acetates. For the best conditions, procyanidine (PAC), flavonoids, terpene trilactones (TTLs), and polyprenyl acetates (PPAs) were extracted at 86.07%, 77.72%, 93.29%, and 94.63%, respectively. Two phase hydrophilic–hydrophobic DES systems were developed to investigate biphasic chiral extraction of threo-nine.25 Eight hydrophobic DESs and six hydrophilic DESs were investigated. Screening of different two phase systems showed that the one of (–)-menthol-L(+)-lactic acid/choline chloride-urea gave the optimum results with a maximum enantiomeric excess value of 31.6%. Three Phase Systems. In 2018, it was claimed that hydrophobic DESs were prepared with levulinic acid, namely, L-menthol-levulinic acid, thymol-levulinic acid, and carvacrol-levulinic acid, all in 1:1, 3:2, and a 2:3 molar ratios. ⁵¹ These were used for the preparation of ternary systems composed of the hydrophobic DES, n-heptane, and methanol. Interestingly, it was found that after equilibrium, the ratio of the HBD and HBA is not the same but changes with initial concentration of the components of the DES in the system. It is assumed that hydrogen bonding between the different components is the driving force. **Removal of Components from Leaves.** In the beginning of 2017, hydrophobic DESs were used for the extraction of Artemisinin, the only effective drug in the treatment for malaria, from *Artemisia annua* leaves. 15 Thirteen DESs were used with methyl trioctylammonium chloride in combination with ethylene glycol, 1-propanol, 1,3-propanediol, glycerol, 1-butanol, 1,2-butanediol, hexyl alcohol, capryl alcohol, decyl alcohol, dodecyl alcohol, 1-tetradecanol, cyclohexanol, and DL-menthol. Since Artemisinin is a compound with moderate hydrophobicity, it was investigated what DES gave the highest extraction efficiency. Moreover, different extraction methods were investigated. The optimization steps showed that 1-butanol with methyl trioctyl ammonium chloride performed the best with a solvent/solid ratio of 17.5:1, ultrasonic power of 180 W, a temperature of 45 °C, a particle size mesh of 80, and an extraction time of 70 min as optimal extraction conditions. These optimized extraction conditions gave an extraction yield of 7.9936 ± 0.0364 mg/g and performed more efficiently than petroleum ether. Another example in 2017 regarding the extraction from leaves was the extraction of polyprenyl acetates from *Ginkgo biloba* leaves. 30 Eighteen hydrophobic DESs were prepared, with methyl trioctylammonium chloride and hexanoic acid, octanoic acid, decanoic acid, dodecanoic acid, myristic acid, palmitic acid, cis-9-octadecenoic acid, ricinoleic acid, 1-propanol, 1-butanol, hexyl alcohol, capryl alcohol, decyl alcohol, dodecyl alcohol, 1- tetradecanol, cyclohexanol, and DL-menthol. After initial tests, the DESs with hexyl alcohol, capryl alcohol, and decyl alcohol gave the best results and were further optimized in molar ratios between the components. It was found that the hydrophobic DES composed of methyltrioctylammonium chloride, capryl alcohol, and octylic acid in a molar ratio of 1:2:3 performed the best. Several extraction methods were tested, which eventually led to an extraction yield of 84.11 ± 0.7366 mg/g. At the start of 2018, DESs based on organic acids and quaternary ammonium salts were used in the microwave-assisted extraction of Baicalin from *Scutellaria baicalensis* Georgi.24 The DESs used throughout this work were decanoic acid:tetrabutylammonium chloride in 2:1, 1:1, and 1:2 molar ratios, decanoic acid:methyltrioctylammonium chloride in 2:1, 1:1, and 1:2 molar ratios, decanoic acid:methyltrioctylammonium bromide in 2:1, 1:1 molar ratios, and decanoic acid:tetraoctylammonium bromide in 2:1 molar ratios. Decanoic acid:tetrabutylammonium chloride (1:2) has the highest extraction yield with 106.96 mg·g⁻¹, which is a similar level as conducted with the pharmacopeia procedure. Interestingly, hydrophobic DESs can also be used to remove phytocannabinoids, such as tetrahydrocannabinol, cannabidiol, and their carboxylated homologues, from raw cannabis plant material.⁶¹ The focus was on the extraction of tetrahydrocannabinol, cannabidiol, and their carboxylated homologues. The hydrophobic DESs used throughout this investigation were produced from terpenes and natural organic acids. All the hydrophobic DESs had a 1:1 molar ratio with menthol used as HBA. The HBDs were formic acid, acetic acid, propionic acid, butyric acid, hexanoic acid, octanoic acid, dodecanoic acid, lactic acid, phenylacetic acid, and mandelic acid. The results showed that the DES composed of acetic acid and menthol performed the best, with extraction efficiencies between 118.6% and 132.6%. Solubility of CO2 in Hydrophobic DESs. An interesting topic addressed with decanoic acid-based hydrophobic DESs is their use as CO2 capture agents.68 Decanoic acid is combined with methyltrioctylammonium chloride, methyltrioctylammonium bromide, tetrabutylammonium chloride, tetraoctylammonium chloride, and tetraoctylammonium bromide in a 2:1 molar ratio. With decanoic acid and tetraoctylammonium chloride, the 1.5:1 molar ratio was tested also. The Henry's law constants for the 1.5:1 molar ratio of decanoic acid:tetraoctylammonium bromide had the highest CO2 solubility equal to the IL [C4mim][BF4], and it was shown that the DES could be reused for multiple cycles. Dietz et al. modeled the solubilities of CO₂ in hydrophobic DESs with Perturbed-Chain Statistical Associating Fluid Theory (PC-SAFT).³⁶,⁷⁸ The PC-SAFT “pseudopure” approach was 10606 https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.0c00559 ACS Sustainable Chem. Eng. 2020, 8, 10591–10612 ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering pubs.acs.org/journal/ascecg Perspective used, and the segment number, temperature-independent segment diameter, and dispersion-energy parameter were determined based on liquid density data only. The hydrophobic DESs that they modeled were decanoic acid with tetraocty- lammonium chloride in a 2:1 molar ratio, decanoic acid with tetraoctylammonium chloride in a 1.5:1 molar ratio, decanoic acid with tetraoctylammonium bromide in a 2:1 molar ratio, perfluorodecanoic acid with tetraoctylammonium chloride in a 2:1 molar ratio, and decanoic acid with tetrabutylammonium chloride in a 2:1 molar ratio. The solubilities of CO2 in the DESs could be predicted reasonably well with a few exceptions at 298.15, 308.15, and 323.15 K. Very recently, experimental and theoretical work has been reported on the use of hydrophobic DESs for the capture of CO2. Ternary DESs were formed by investigation combinations between dodecanoic acid, decanoic acid, oleic acid, and tetrabutylammonium bromide. Two ternary DESs were presented: the combination of tetrabutylammonium bromide with dodecanoic acid and decanoic acid and the combination of tetrabutylammonium bromide with dodecanoic acid and decanoic acid.75 They presented comparable CO2 solubilities as presented before in this paragraph, but they used higher CO2 pressures. Interestingly, in the IL field, the nonidealities of binary mixtures of ILs have been investigated on physical absorption for the capture of CO₂. v It was concluded that positive deviation from ideal behavior were observed that could be used to enhance the physical absorption for CO₂ capture. This behavior should also be further investigated to see whether the solubility of DESs can be increased. **Formation of Hydrogels.** Interestingly, by using a sodium DES, it was possible to form a supramolecular hydrogel.58 A DES phase consisting of a 4:1 molar ratio of decanoic acid to dodecanoate sodium salt was used. Different regimes were found when this DES was mixed with water under variation of temperature, such as a solid, clear gel, turbid gel, two liquid phases, and a homogeneous liquid. Thus, it depends on composition and temperature what phase is formed, and it can be debated if it is truly a hydrophobic DES. It was mentioned that the physicochemical properties density and viscosity of this DES were more similar to hydrophobic than hydrophilic DESs. Finally, it was found that the viscosity is thermoreversible and depends on the water content. Formation of Oil-in-Water Emulsions with Hydrophobic DESs. The hydrophobic DES 1-tetradecanol and menthol in a 1:2 molar ratio is investigated for the production of oil-in-water emulsions with sodium dodecyl sulfate as the surfactant.55 It was shown that a linear correlation exists between the time and the droplet growth (d³). Influences on the droplet growth of the surfactant concentration and the mass percentage of the DES to the water phase was investigated. The results of the hydrophobic DES as the oil phase were compared with decane as the oil phase. Interestingly, the droplet growth of the DES was lower than the one of decane, while the solubility of the DES in the water phase is many factors larger. It was shown that the DES system should not be treated as a new system but as a two component mixture and so the growth rate depends on the solubility of the less soluble component. Ideally, by using very insoluble components with a very soluble component a rather stable emulsion can be formed. So, its potential is enormous to disperse components as emulsions within an aqueous environment. Hydrophobic DESs and Their Use in Wound Healing. Hydrophobic DESs composed of menthol in combination with lauric acid, stearic acid, and myristic acid with different molar ratios were investigated for their wound healing abilities.74 It was shown that menthol combined with stearic acid in a 8:1 molar ratio has the lowest cytotoxicity. In general, it is concluded that menthol and stearic acid has the highest potential. **Membrane Formation.** Hydrophobic DESs were used as additives for PES membranes, more specifically decanoic acid with tetrabutylammonium chloride in a 2:1 molar ratio.²⁶ Surprisingly, with the addition of only 2 wt % of DES, the water flux of the membrane increased to 142.84 L/(m²·h), 4.65 times higher than the flux through the pure PES membrane. These hydrophobic DESs were combined with the membranes 16P10A, M3203B, and PP2E-[HF]. It was found that by addition of DES to the membrane, the transport of furfural and hydroxymethylfurfural increased. **Centrifugal Partition Chromatography.** A quaternary solvent system composed of n-heptane, methanol, and the DES L-menthol with levulinic acid in a 1:1 molar ratio was used for centrifugal partition chromatography, in which it was tested whether the phases can be used as mobile and stationary phases.⁶³ It was found that the DES components were present in both phases. From the partition coefficient, it was concluded that the hydrophobic components were usable for centrifugal partition chromatography. Up to 79.1% of stationary phase retention was found. Formation of a Ferrofluid. A menthol-based hydrophobic DES was combined with magnetic clay to form a ferrofluid. 48 This was coupled with directly suspended microextraction to remove explosives from water and soil samples. A long list of fatty acids in combination with DL-menthol was tested, of which the following formed a liquid phase: decanoic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), octanoic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), oleic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), dodecanoic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), valeric acid:DL-menthol (2:1), propionic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), lactic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), butyric acid:DL-menthol (2:1), acrylic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), and acetic acid:DL-menthol (2:1). CHALLENGES AND LIMITATIONS OF HYDROPHOBIC DESS In the last 5 years, many hydrophobic DESs and various applications have been presented into the scientific literature. However, overall, it can be concluded that a major disadvantage is a lack of fundamental knowledge. It is of high importance that a proper definition of DESs be presented, which will also help to discriminate between true "deep eutectics" and merely "eutectics". First attempts have been made, but it is good if the community would come to a consensus. It is debatable whether fundamental differences between a "deep eutectic" vs a "eutectic" makes a large difference application-wise. Although when the solid-liquid equilibria are not known, it can be tricky since solidification can occur with the smallest change in molar ratio of the DES component. Next to the solid-liquid equilibria, also the liquid-vapor equilibria should be further investigated. It is usually stated in the scientific literature that DESs are nonvolatile. However, this will depend on the components that are used and their interactions. For example, when acetic acid is used as one of the DES components, it makes common sense that the volatility is not neglectable. Regarding the liquid-liquid equilibria, these should not be taken lightly. With the addition of an aqueous phase and a solute, very complex quaternary or quinary systems are formed, which can be very challenging. An aspect that can help to understand the fundamentals and basics of DESs is the use of theory, molecular modeling, and simulations. These aspects can strengthen the investigation of the DES field and explore the proposed factors that form a DES. A problem related to the whole DES field is the recycling of the DESs after applications, an investigated area. This topic should be a major point of interest to ensure that DESs will have a scientific and industrial future. A type of recycling that is currently investigated is back extraction, but it is debatable if this is the best method of recycling. Most likely, new and innovative methods have to be devised to improve the recycling of the DESs. Another point that should be addressed for the whole field of DESs is further investigation into their toxicity and biodegrad- ability. Even when presenting DESs that are merely prepared with natural components, it is still a question if they are not toxic for the environment and the populations of the world. A challenge truly related to hydrophobic DESs is the question whether a DES is actually hydrophobic. Many papers in the field of hydrophobic DESs use components that should not be considered as hydrophobic, for example, acetic acid and lactic acid. A limitation related to hydrophobic DESs is the contami- nation of the water phase with the DES components. An important question to answer is the effect that this contamination will have on the water phase and, for example, the environment and life forms in this water phase. Most likely, the organics should be removed from the water phase. This will be a very difficult task since these concentrations are rather low. Something interesting that is only hardly investigated is the long stability of DESs, especially between the combinations of the solid components and during prolonged use. Only recently it was investigated what the effects could be when an acid with an alcohol were mixed to form a liquid phase. It was shown that the acid and the alcohol react, 77 which basically says that it is no longer a combination of two solid components. Thus, it is not a DES anymore. Moreover, it is interesting to investigate if solid formation will occur within the solvent over a longer period of time. From an industrial aspect, a factor as corrosivity is of interest. In general, it can be concluded that hydrophobic DESs have some unique properties and applications that make them very interesting solvents for future use in academics and industry. It is best to consider hydrophobic DESs not as the next generation of hydrophobic ILs but as a new sustainable solvent, with their own properties, applications, and challenges. 10608 https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.0c00559 ACS Sustainable Chem. Kroon (1980) obtained her M.Sc. (2004) and Ph.D. (2006) in Chemical Engineering from TU Delft, Netherlands. She was awarded the prize for best graduate student and the DSM Science & Technology Award. Thereafter, she worked as Assistant Professor at TU Delft, MATGAS Research Center in Spain, and Stanford University in the USA. In 2011, she was appointed Full Professor at Eindhoven University of Technology as the youngest female professor in The Netherlands. In 2015, she was awarded the Science Talent Award of the year by the journal New Scientist. Dr. Kroon joined Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi as a professor in January 2016. Her research focuses on the development of novel energy-efficient affinity separation processes (e.g., aromatic/aliphatic separation, gas sweetening, desalination) on the basis of phase behavior. So far, she has published around 130 articles and has over 3500 citations. She is also an associate editor of Journal of Chemical & Engineering Data. ## REFERENCES (1) Abbott, A. G. P. van Osch,* Carin H. J. T. Dietz, Samah E. E. Warrag, and Maaike C. Kroon* Cite This: ACS Sustainable Chem. Eng. 2020, 8, 10591–10612 Read Online ACCESS | <::transcription of the content : chart::> Metrics & More | <::transcription of the content : chart::> Article Recommendations ABSTRACT: Hydrophobic deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are a new generation of water immiscible solvents that have been presented in the literature for the first time in 2015. These solvents have been used for many applications. Here, an overview is given regarding hydrophobic DESs with their physicochemical properties, applications, and the challenges and limitations that the field currently is experiencing. First, a general introduction and an introduction to hydrophobic DESs are presented to explain more about DESs, their origin, and hydrophobic ones. Here, also, an overview of all the hydrophobic DESs presented in the literature is given. After the introduction, physicochemical properties such as density, viscosity, melting point, degradation temperature, volatilities, and solvatochromic properties are discussed. It is continued with the discussion of 21 different applications of hydrophobic DESs. In general, applications related to liquid-liquid extractions, liquid-liquid microextractions, formation of two and three phase systems, removal of components from leaves, gas-liquid extractions, formation of hydrogels, membrane formation, centrifugal partition chromatography, formation of a ferrofluid, coating, photoluminescence, and dye-sensitized solar cells, and catalysis have been investigated. Finally, challenges and limitations of hydrophobic DESs are discussed. <::A magnifying glass, drawn in black outline, magnifies a small glass vial. The vial contains an orange liquid, filling approximately the bottom third of the vial. The vial is sitting on a reflective surface and casts a shadow behind it. The background is a plain, light color. : figure::> KEYWORDS: Hydrophobic deep eutectic solvents, Densities, Viscosities, Melting points, Degradation temperatures, Volatilities, Solvatochromic properties, Applications ## INTRODUCTION Recently, the inceptions of sustainability, green chemistry, and engineering principles have been the pillars to achieve economic and environmental goals in both industry and academia. In simple words, research is directed towards the design of sustainable and green processes that are based on the exploitation of innovative and renewable resources, which are in balance with the least economic and environmental impacts. The design and applications of sustainable solvent media have been a hot topic in different scientific areas. Breakthrough advances in obtaining solvent alternatives to toxic and volatile organic solvents have been achieved, like the application of ionic liquids, supercritical carbon dioxide, and deep eutectic solvents (DESs), first introduced in 2003.¹ Here, we present a comprehensive overview into hydrophobic DESs, innovative solvents presented for the first time in the literature in 2015.²,³ ## INTRODUCTION TO HYDROPHOBIC DESS DESs are eutectic mixtures that have been presented in the literature as designer solvents that could be an alternative solvent class to ionic liquids (ILs).¹ ILs have been defined as salts with the combination of an organic cation and anion with a melting point lower than 100 °C, often liquid at room temperature.⁴ Finding a definition for DESs is a more daunting task. No clear and uniform definition has been reported by the major review papers on DESs, although several attempts were performed.⁵⁻⁸ DESs are usually described as a combination of two or more solids that upon mixing form a liquid phase. It has been anticipated that entropy of mixing, van der Waals interactions, and hydrogen bonding plays a role in the formation of DESs. Recently, two papers were presented in the literature that investigated the phase diagrams of DESs, which correlated the phase behavior and the deepness of the eutectic point to the definition of DESs.⁹,¹⁰ As expected, interactions between the components of the DES have an influence on the deepness of the eutectic point as clearly shown by the phase diagrams. Kollau et al. used regular solution theory to predict the phase diagrams and showed that some combinations of two solid components could be predicted with ideal phase behavior, while some have a clear deep eutectic.¹⁰ It is stated that a eutectic mixture can only be considered as a DES when the melting point of the mixture is significantly lower than the one of the ideal prediction. for DESs.⁹ An aspect of high importance is the fact that DESs are mixtures of two or more components and not one pure salt consisting of ions. Thus, treating DESs as the new generation of ILs makes no sense due to the large differences. Moreover, it is stated that it is debatable whether a combination of a solid and a liquid component is actually a DES; it might be a solvolysis instead. The biggest debate is on the eutectic composition of a DES, the deepness of the eutectic point, and how to define this. In the end, Martins et al. decided on the following definition: "A deep eutectic solvent a mixture of two or more pure compounds for which the eutectic point temperature is below that of an ideal liquid mixture, presenting significant negative deviations from ideality. Additionally, the temperature depression should be such that the mixture is liquid at operating temperature for a certain composition range. Otherwise, a simpler term "eutectic solvent" could be used to describe mixtures that do not fulfill these criteria." This is a solid start to further discuss the definition of (hydrophobic) DESs. Recently, a new class of DESs, type V, has been introduced into the literature.¹¹ This type V class makes the field of (hydrophobic) DESs a little bit more clear. Type V DESs are composed solely of molecular substances. More specifically, it is reported that a hydrogen bond acceptor undergoes hydrogen bonding with a hydroxyl compound that is attached to an aromatic ring, for example, a phenolic compound.¹¹ In this perspective, all the combinations of two solid components presented in the literature as hydrophobic DESs are given. However, the term "hydrophobic" should also not be taken lightly, and it might be best to put some constraints on it too. Nowadays, components such as acetic acid and lactic acid have been presented as compounds of hydrophobic DESs, as can be read in this perspective, while they have relatively high solubility in water. In the literature, also the name NADES (natural deep eutectic solvents) is used on many occasions.⁷ We think it should be a goal of the DES field itself to produce solvents with natural and safe components. It is often stated that DESs have many advantages over conventional solvents, such as easy preparation, no need of purification, and tunability of properties.⁴ These can, in general, be considered as true. For hydrophobic DESs, it can also be given that they are water immiscible, although for this property it should be mentioned that this mainly depends on the compounds and their hydrophobicity. Often DESs are also mentioned as biodegradable,⁴ but one should not forget that this will be determined by the components that are used and their synergetic effect. The fact that (hydrophobic) DESs have a lower volatility is recently proven, but also for this property, it truly depends on the components that are used for a certain DES.¹² The field of hydrophobic DESs is now almost five years old and has evolved during this time. It started with two publications in 2015 where the first hydrophobic DESs were presented and used for liquid–liquid extractions. 2,3 These were hydrophobic DESs that were far from ideal at that moment with high viscosities and large amounts of DES components that leached to the water phase. In 2016, still only a few papers were presented, but the very impressive work on the removal of metals from an aqueous environment was started. 13,14 The year 2017 was really a year of growth for the hydrophobic DES field. Some very interesting applications that were investigated include the extraction of Artemisinin, a medicine for malaria, from *Artemisia* *annua* leaves, 15 the first microextractions, 16 photon upconver- sion, 17 and the use of hydrophobic DESs in membranes. 18 In the years after, a rapid growth of the field was observed. Some interesting papers are, for example, related to theoretical approaches, 10 determination of the liquid phase behavior, 19 and the introduction of the type V DESs, specifically introduced for hydrophobic DESs. 11 A full overview of all hydrophobic DESs presented so far in the literature is shown in Table 1. However, it should be mentioned that this will all depend on the components chosen, and its potential will most likely also depend on the application that can be performed with them. ## PHYSICOCHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF HYDROPHOBIC DESS The physicochemical properties and thermal stabilities of all reported hydrophobic DESs so far are presented in the following sections. **Density.** Density (ρ) is one of the essential properties for solvent design and applications. In principle, the densities of DESs are related to the molecular packing and the interactions between its constituents. Table 2 lists the density data of the hydrophobic DESs reported in the literature. From Table 2, it can be observed that the hydrophobic DESs show a density between 0.88 and 1.5 g·cm⁻³. A proportional relationship of the density and its constituents is evident for the components of the DESs at the molar ratios. As an example, for menthol-based DESs at molar ratio (1:1), the hydrophobic DESs densities followed the order menthol:salol > menthol:acetic acid > menthol:octanoic acid > menthol:decanoic acid, which is the same order of the component 2's densities. However, no final conclusion can be drawn, and further experimental measurements are needed for a broader range of DES combinations at the same molar ratios. Furthermore, for the same component 2 and molar ratio, the density of the hydrophobic DESs decreases with increasing the alkyl chain length of component 1. The density of ammonium-based DESs in a molar ratio of (component 1:component 2 = 1:2) follows the order tetrabutylammonium chloride:decanoic acid > tetraheptylammonium chloride:decanoic acid > tetraoctylammonium chloride:decanoic acid. Furthermore, van Osch et al. have tested the change in densities after mixing with water. The results showed a slight influence of the DES density due to the low water uptake.⁴¹ Additionally, a linear decrease of the DES density with temperature was reported by Ribeiro et al.³ **Viscosity.** The viscosity of the solvents is one of the determinant factors in its selection especially for an industrial- scale application. It is expected that DESs are formed via hydrogen bonding interactions, limiting the mobility of the DESs molecules; therefore, high DES viscosities are expected. However, viscosities as low as 7 mPa·s were reported for the hydrophobic DES dodecanoic acid:octanoic acid (1:3) (Table 2). All the viscosities of the hydrophobic DESs reported so far are listed in Table 3. It can be seen that the hydrophobic DESs have a large range of viscosities (~7-86,800 mPa·s). This allows big room for task-oriented solvent design. The chemical nature and the interactions between the DES constituents are the main factors affecting the viscosity. It should be mentioned that no straightforward relation can be found in viscosities for the same HBA with different HBDs at fixed molar ratio. Moreover, it was observed that the viscosity changes significantly with temper- ature. The increase in temperature leads to a substantial decrease in viscosity following an Arrhenius-like behavior. **Melting Point.** The melting point of a DES is the lowest temperature at which the solvent could be applied in liquid state. By general definition, the DESs exhibit a melting point that is far below that of its individual constituents. Table 4 lists the melting temperatures (_T_m) of hydrophobic DESs reported in the literature. It can be observed that the melting points of all hydrophobic DESs studied are well below room temperature. Few hydrophobic DESs (i.e., menthol:pyruvic acid and menthol:dodecanoic acid) exhibited two melting points; however, both temperatures are well below that of both constituents (Table 4). The melting point is highly dependent on the structure and strength of the interactions between the HBD and HBA. A problem within the field of hydrophobic DES is the presumption of melting points. Often a ratio between two solid points is considered as the eutectic point as soon as the combination of two solid components becomes liquid. However, the melting points should be determined by investigating the full solid–liquid phase behavior to find its true eutectic point. Recently, new investigations showed the use of phase diagrams to determine the composition at the eutectic point and its melting point. For example, phase diagrams of menthol with octanoic acid, decanoic acid, dodecanoic acid, myristic acid, palmitic acid, and stearic acid were tested. ⁵³ This is the way forward for the field of hydrophobic DESs. Like the melting point of DESs, the degradation behavior of DESs is highly dependent on the nature of the DES constituents. **Volatilities.** Recently, a new physicochemical property of hydrophobic DESs was determined, namely, volatility. ^12 The total vapor pressure of six hydrophobic DESs was tested, namely, decanoic acid:thymol (1:1), decanoic acid:lidocaine (2:1), decanoic acid:lidocaine (3:1), decanoic acid:lidocaine (4:1), decanoic acid:menthol (1:1), and thymol:lidocaine in a 2:1 molar ratio. The most volatile DES was the one composed of decanoic acid and menthol, with a volatility that is 150–1000 times smaller than toluene in the temperature region of 320–380 K. ^12 This research with the first preliminary results on the volatilities shows that volatility is an important factor to further investigate in the future for hydrophobic and hydrophilic DESs. **Solvatochromic Properties.** In 2018, intermolecular interactions by using solvatochromic probes for hydrophobic and hydrophilic DESs was explored.²¹ The hydrophobic DESs investigated were levulinic acid:tetrabutylammonium chloride (2:1), octanoic acid:tetrabutylammonium chloride (2:1), decanoic acid:tetrabutylammonium chloride (2:1), dodecanoic acid:tetrabutylammonium chloride (2:1), levulinic acid:DL- Menthol (1:1), octanoic acid:DL-Menthol (1:1), dodecanoic acid:DL-Menthol (1:2), and acetic:DL-Menthol (1:1). The intermolecular interactions were measured with the Kamlet- Taft parameters. The Kamlet-Taft α, β, π*, and EᴛN were evaluated. Overall, it was found that the DESs have a high hydrogen bond acidity, caused by the acids, and not much variation in hydrogen bonding basicity if the same compound as HBA was used. As expected, substantial differences were found in hydrogen bonding basicity when the HBA was varied. Of the tested DESs, the HBA controlled the dipolarity/polarizability. Surprisingly, DESs showed higher hydrogen bonding donating and accepting ability in comparison to ILs and conventional solvents. Furthermore, DESs composed of a combination between the acids octanoic, decanoic, dodecanoic, myristic, palmitic, and stearic acids and the terpenes L(-)-menthol and thymol were tested. ⁵³ Also here, solvatochromic parameters were investigated with the Kamlet-Taft parameters, from which it could be concluded that the chosen terpene had the biggest influence on the parameters. Moreover, thymol induced a higher hydrogen bond acidity, while menthol increased the hydrogen bond basicity. Recently, the Kamlet-Taft parameters of the combinations of menthol + thymol, menthol + camphor, menthol + borneol, menthol + sobrerol, thymol + camphor, thymol + borneol, and thymol + sobrerol were studied.⁵⁴ The results showed that thymol has a higher polarizability/dipolarity due to the presence of its aromatic ring. Moreover, it was found that there is a variation between the hydrogen bond donating and accepting ability. Really interesting was the tunability of the α, β, and π* behavior found for menthol + thymol and thymol + camphor combinations. All the applications are further discussed in the paragraphs given below. Many of the presented applications are liquid-liquid extractions, which form quite complicated systems. The hydrophobic DES itself is already a binary or a ternary system. With the addition of an aqueous phase and a solute, quaternary or quinary systems are formed, which tend to have all kinds of interactions and thermodynamic effects. Removal of Volatile Fatty Acids from Water. Hydrophobic DESs were discovered in 2015.2,3 Despite the field of hydrophobic DESs being relatively young, some applications have been presented in the literature. The first application tested for hydrophobic DESs was the removal of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) from water. Hydrophobic DESs based on decanoic acid and a variation of quaternary ammonium salts were used as solvent, while the VFAs acetic, propionic, and butyric acids were used as pollutants of the water phase.2 The results are depicted in Table 8. They show that all developed hydrophobic DESs outperform the industrial standard trioctylamine and that with an increase in the chain length of the VFA the extraction efficiency increases. More specifically, decanoic acid:methyl-trioctylammonium bromide (2:1) had the highest extraction efficiency for the VFAs, most likely since the methyl group induces lower steric hindrance. An exception to these results was found for propionic acid and butyric acid for the DES decanoic acid:tetraheptylammonium chloride (2:1). Most likely, the extraction efficiencies of this DES were higher due to turbidities in the water phase after centrifugation, an indication that no proper phase separation occurred. Moreover, the results showed that a change from bromide to chloride anion gave a decrease in the extraction efficiency, caused by an increase in steric hindrance. After the start of research into the applications of hydrophobic DESs in 2015, two papers regarding hydrophobic DESs and their applications were reported in 2016, both on the extraction of metal ions from an aqueous environment. 13,14 Tereshatov et al. reported on indium extraction with four hydrophobic DESs, i.e., tetraheptylammonium chloride:ibuprofen (7:3), tetraheptylam- monium chloride:oleic acid (1:2), tetraheptylammonium chloride:decanoic acid (1:2), and DL-menthol:dodecanoic acid (2:1).14 A kinetic study was performed to determine the time to equilibrium between the metal species in the DES phase and the water phase. It was found that this was after 5 min of shaking. The effect of a variation in HCl concentration and oxalic acid concentration on distribution coefficient was investigated. The results of the hydrophobic DES as the oil phase were compared with decane as the oil phase. Interestingly, the droplet growth of the DES was lower than the one of decane, while the solubility of the DES in the water phase is many factors larger. It was shown that the DES system should not be treated as a new system but as a two component mixture and so the growth rate depends on the solubility of the less soluble component. Ideally, by using very insoluble components with a very soluble component a rather stable emulsion can be formed. So, its potential is enormous to disperse components as emulsions within an aqueous environment. Hydrophobic DESs and Their Use in Wound Healing. Hydrophobic DESs composed of menthol in combination with lauric acid, stearic acid, and myristic acid with different molar ratios were investigated for their wound healing abilities.74 It was shown that menthol combined with stearic acid in a 8:1 molar ratio has the lowest cytotoxicity. In general, it is concluded that menthol and stearic acid has the highest potential. **Membrane Formation.** Hydrophobic DESs were used as additives for PES membranes, more specifically decanoic acid with tetrabutylammonium chloride in a 2:1 molar ratio.²⁶ Surprisingly, with the addition of only 2 wt % of DES, the water flux of the membrane increased to 142.84 L/(m²·h), 4.65 times higher than the flux through the pure PES membrane. Rejection rates of pepsin, egg albumin, and bovine serum albumin were measured. They were 91.5%, 97.3%, and 99.0%, respectively. Moreover, liquid membranes supported with a hydrophobic DES were tested for removal of furfural hydroxymethylfurfural from an aquatic environment. 18 The hydrophobic DESs tested in this work were decanoic acid:tetraoctylammonium bromide (2:1), decanoic acid:thymol (1:1), decanoic acid:menthol (1:1), and thymol:lidocaine (2:1). These hydrophobic DESs were combined with the membranes 16P10A, M3203B, and PP2E-[HF]. It was found that by addition of DES to the membrane, the transport of furfural and hydroxymethylfurfural increased. **Centrifugal Partition Chromatography.** A quaternary solvent system composed of n-heptane, methanol, and the DES L-menthol with levulinic acid in a 1:1 molar ratio was used for centrifugal partition chromatography, in which it was tested whether the phases can be used as mobile and stationary phases.⁶³ It was found that the DES components were present in both phases. From the partition coefficient, it was concluded that the hydrophobic components were usable for centrifugal partition chromatography. Up to 79.1% of stationary phase retention was found. Formation of a Ferrofluid. A menthol-based hydrophobic DES was combined with magnetic clay to form a ferrofluid. 48 This was coupled with directly suspended microextraction to remove explosives from water and soil samples. A long list of fatty acids in combination with DL-menthol was tested, of which the following formed a liquid phase: decanoic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), octanoic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), oleic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), dodecanoic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), valeric acid:DL-menthol (2:1), propionic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), lactic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), butyric acid:DL-menthol (2:1), acrylic acid:DL-menthol (2:1), and acetic acid:DL-menthol (2:1). The ferrofluid was made by mixing 50 mg of MMT@Fe3O4 magnetic nanoparticles with 1 mL of DES. Many effects were explored, such as the influence of DES type, salt addition, equilibrium time, and many more. The explosives tested were 2-nitrotoluene, 3-nitrotoluene, 1,2-dinitrobenzene, 1,3,5-trinitrobenzene, 2,6-dinitrotoluene, 2,4-dinitrotoluene, 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene, cyclotetramethylene tetranitramine, cyclotrimethylene-trinitramine, hexanitrohexaazaisowurtzitane, tetryl, and pentaerythritol tetranitrate. They found that the recoveries were between 88% and 104%. **Coatings.** A hydrophobic DES was also used as an additive for sol–gel sorbent coatings of poly(dimethylsiloxane) fiber to determine the amount of toluene, ethylbenzene, and o-xylene in water.66 Three hydrophobic DESs were prepared, i.e., 4-hydroxybenzoate:methyltrioctylammonium chloride (2:1), ethyl 4-hydroxybenzoate:methyl trioctylammonium chloride (1:1), and ethyl 4-hydroxybenzoate:methyltrioctylammonium chloride (1:2). The hydrophobic DESs decanoic acid:tetrabutylammonium chloride in 1:1, 2:1, 3:1, and 5:1 molar ratios and decanoic acid:tetraoctylammonium chloride in a 3:1 molar ratio were used. It was shown that the samples have high thermal stabilities, and a photon upconversion yield of 0.11–0.21 was found. Three DESs, of which one was a hydrophobic DES, were used for induced circularly polarized luminescence. DESs composed of tetrabutylammonium chloride and L- and D-glutamic acid, L-proline, and L-arginine were used. 29 To measure the induced circularly polarized luminescence, a racemic mixture of dissymmetric lathanide complexes, i.e., europium, terbium, and samarium were dissolved. It was concluded that DESs, and so the hydrophobic DES, can be used as a solvent for chiral light emitting materials. By a variation in the DES components, its capability could be controlled. The hydrophobic DES composed of acetic acid and DL- menthol was tested for its use as an electrolyte medium in the design of eco-sustainable dye sensitized solar cells.⁴⁹ It was concluded that the photovoltage was higher in comparison to commonly used volatile organic compounds. Moreover, it was suggested that an important role can be played by hydrophobic eutectic mixtures. **Catalysis.** Hydrophilic and hydrophobic DESs were investigated for the production of aldols.38 More specifically, the catalytic aldose activity was tested on 4-nitrobenzaldehyde and acetone with the porcine pancreas lipase. Four DESs were tested, i.e., glycerol:choline chloride (1.5:1), ethylene glycol:tetraoctylammonium bromide (3:1), 1,5-pentadiol:tetraoctylammonium bromide (3:1), and 4-nitrobenzaldehyde:tetrabutylammonium chloride (1.5:2.2). It was concluded that especially in hydrophobic DESs the desired aldol product was prepared. However, it was also shown that the conventional solvent acetone outperformed the DESs. An interesting concept that was presented in 2018 where the DES has a double function acting both as solvent and product.47 The fatty acids octanoic, decanoic, and dodecanoic acids were combined with (-)-menthol in molar ratios of 0.45:0.55, 0.35:0.65, and 0.25:0.75 at the start of the experiment. Six lipases were used, two immobilized and four solid ones. The lipases N534, c-LEcta CALB, CRL, BCL, PCL, and PFL were used. The addition of water to the reaction mixture induced the outcome of the reaction. The outcome of the addition of 10% water led to 50%, 83%, and 71% of octanoic, decanoic, and dodecanoic acids after 7 days, respectively. CHALLENGES AND LIMITATIONS OF HYDROPHOBIC DESS In the last 5 years, many hydrophobic DESs and various applications have been presented into the scientific literature. However, overall, it can be concluded that a major disadvantage is a lack of fundamental knowledge. It is of high importance that a proper definition of DESs be presented, which will also help to discriminate between true "deep eutectics" and merely "eutectics". First attempts have been made, but it is good if the community would come to a consensus. It is debatable whether fundamental differences between a "deep eutectic" vs a "eutectic" makes a large difference application-wise. Although when the solid-liquid equilibria are not known, it can be tricky since solidification can occur with the smallest change in molar ratio of the DES component. Next to the solid-liquid equilibria, also the liquid-vapor equilibria should be further investigated. It is usually stated in the scientific literature that DESs are nonvolatile. However, this will depend on the components that are used and their interactions. For example, when acetic acid is used as one of the DES components, it makes common sense that the volatility is not neglectable. Regarding the liquid-liquid equilibria, these should not be taken lightly. With the addition of an aqueous phase and a solute, very complex quaternary or quinary systems are formed, which can be very challenging. An aspect that can help to understand the fundamentals and basics of DESs is the use of theory, molecular modeling, and simulations. These aspects can strengthen the investigation of the DES field and explore the proposed factors that form a DES. A problem related to the whole DES field is the recycling of the DESs after applications, an investigated area. This topic should be a major point of interest to ensure that DESs will have a scientific and industrial future. A type of recycling that is currently investigated is back extraction, but it is debatable if this is the best method of recycling. Most likely, new and innovative methods have to be devised to improve the recycling of the DESs. Another point that should be addressed for the whole field of DESs is further investigation into their toxicity and biodegrad- ability. Even when presenting DESs that are merely prepared with natural components, it is still a question if they are not toxic for the environment and the populations of the world. A challenge truly related to hydrophobic DESs is the question whether a DES is actually hydrophobic. Many papers in the field of hydrophobic DESs use components that should not be considered as hydrophobic, for example, acetic acid and lactic acid. A limitation related to hydrophobic DESs is the contami- nation of the water phase with the DES components. An important question to answer is the effect that this contamination will have on the water phase and, for example, the environment and life forms in this water phase. Most likely, the organics should be removed from the water phase. This will be a very difficult task since these concentrations are rather low. Something interesting that is only hardly investigated is the long stability of DESs, especially between the combinations of the solid components and during prolonged use. Only recently it was investigated what the effects could be when an acid with an alcohol were mixed to form a liquid phase. It was shown that the acid and the alcohol react, 77 which basically says that it is no longer a combination of two solid components. Thus, it is not a DES anymore. Moreover, it is interesting to investigate if solid formation will occur within the solvent over a longer period of time. From an industrial aspect, a factor as corrosivity is of interest. In general, it can be concluded that hydrophobic DESs have some unique properties and applications that make them very interesting solvents for future use in academics and industry. It is best to consider hydrophobic DESs not as the next generation of hydrophobic ILs but as a new sustainable solvent, with their own properties, applications, and challenges. 10608 https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.0c00559 ACS Sustainable Chem.
